blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
• Coordination compounds consist of a central metal atom or ion surrounded by neutral molecules, cations or anions known as ligands.

• These compounds exhibit unique properties due to the specific arrangement and

bonding of ligands around the central metal atom.

Terminology of complex compounds

Definitions

Complex ion :

An aggregate of metal ions with anions, cations or neutral molecules is called a complex ion.

Central metal ion :

• The metal ion which forms a complex ion in combination with anions, cations or neutral molecules is called the central metal ion.

• Central metal ion acts as an electron pair acceptor and forms coordinate bond with ligands.

Coordination number :

• From every ligand central metal ion accepts electron pairs. Thus, the number of electron pairs accepted by the central metal ion in the formation of a complex is called as coordination number.

• The total number of coordinate bonds formed by a central metal ion with donor species is called the coordination number of a central metal ion.

Coordination sphere (entity) :

• The central metal atom and the ligands directly attached to it are collectively termed as the coordination sphere.

• Coordination sphere is written inside square brackets, for example [Co(NH3)6]3+

• The part outside the bracket is called ionisation sphere.

• The species present in the coordination sphere are nonionizable.

• The species present in the ionization sphere are ionisable.

Oxidation state :

• It is a number which represents the electric charge on the central metal atom of a complex ion.

• Ex. the oxidation number of Fe, Co and Ni in [Fe(CN)6]4-, [Co(NH3)6]3+, and Ni(CO)4  is +2, +3 and zero, respectively.

Charge on the complex ion :

It is the algebraic sum of the total charge of the ligands and central metal ion.

Ligands :

• The anions, cations or neutral molecules which combine with central metal ion to form complex ion are called as ligands.

• They act as electron pair donor (Lewis bases), but ligands like $CO$ $CN^-$  these can accept electron pairs from the metal ion, because these ligands are $\pi$acids.

blocks.title: Formulas & Mathematical Relations
blocks.text:
Effective Atomic Number (EAN)

Formula: $\text{EAN}=\text{Atomic number of metal}-\text{Oxidation state of metal}+2\times\text{Coordination number}$

blocks.title: Common Misconception
blocks.text: Confusing the coordination number with the oxidation state of the metal.

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question: Calculate the EAN for $[Co(NH_3)_6]^{+3}$.
blocks.answer:
EAN = 36

Atomic No. of Co = 27

Oxidation State of Co = +3

No. of ligands = 6

EAN = 27 - 3 + 2(6)

= 27 - 3 + 12

= 36

blocks.title: Example-2
blocks.question:
Question: The EAN of Fe in the complex [ Fe(CN)6]4- is:

  • 36
  • 34
  • 32
  • 30
blocks.answer:
Solution:

  • The atomic number of Fe = 26
  • The oxidation state of Fe in [ Fe(CN)6]4- is +2
  • Remaining electrons = 26- 2 = 24
  • Each CN-  ligand contributes 2 electrons
EAN = 24+(6*2) =24+12 = 36

Correct Answer is: (1) 36

modules.name: Types of Coordination Compounds and Ligands

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Based on the type of ligands, complex compounds are divided as follows:

• Homoleptic complexes :

A complex in which all the ligands are identical is called Homoleptic complex .

Ex. [Co(NH3)6]2+

• Heteroleptic complexes :

A  complex in which all the ligands are not identical is known as a Heteroleptic complex.

Ex. [Fe(en)2Cl2]1+

Ligands: Species donating electron pairs to metal.

blocks.title: Formulas & Mathematical Relations
blocks.text:
• Coordination Number (CN):
$$CN = The total number of coordinate bonds formed by central metal ion with ligands.

blocks.title: DATA
blocks.text: Types  of ligands

blocks.title: Common Misconceptions
blocks.text:
• Misconception: Metals oxidation state is equal to coordination number.
  • Clarification: Coordination number pertains to ligand donor atoms;
oxidation state involves electron transfer.

  • Misconception: All ligands are neutral.
  • Clarification: Ligands can be anionic, cationic, or neutral, e.g., Cl⁻ is anionic.

blocks.question: What is the coordination number of Cr  in [ Cr(C2O4)3]3- is:
blocks.answer:
Solution:

  • C2O42-( oxalate ion) is a bidentate ligand, meaning it forms two bonds with the central metal ion
  • In [ Cr(C2O4)3]3-, there are 3 oxalate ions, each containing 2 bonds.
Coordination number = 3*2= 6

blocks.title: Example-2
blocks.question:
What is the correct IUPAC name of the complex $[Co(\text{NH}_3)_5\text{Cl}]\text{Cl}_2$ ?

A. Pentamminechloridocobalt(III) chloride
B. Pentachloridoamminecobalt(III) chloride
C. Pentachloridochlorocobalt(III) chloride
D. Pentamminechlorocobaltate(III) chloride
blocks.answer:
Answer: A. Pentamminechloridocobalt(III) chloride

Solution:

  • The ligands are named alphabetically: "ammine" (for $NH_3$​) comes before "chlorido" (for Cl).
  • The metal is cobalt, and its oxidation state is indicated in Roman numerals as (III).
  • The counter ion ($Cl_2$) is written as "chloride."
Thus, the name of the complex is:
Pentamminechloridocobalt(III) chloride.

modules.name: Structural Aspects : Valence Bond Theory (VBT) and Geometry

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Valence Bond Theory (VBT)

  • Formation of coordination compounds by orbital overlap.
  • Involves coordinate bonding through metal and ligand orbitals.
Geometry : Specific geometries based on coordination number and ligand type.

blocks.title: Formulas & Mathematical Relations
blocks.text:
• Coordination Number Calculation:
  • Determined by counting the number of direct metal-ligand bonds.
  • Example: For $[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3+}$, coordination number = 6.
  • Geometry Determination:
  • $CN=2$: Linear
  • $CN=4$: Tetrahedral or Square Planar (common for $d^8$ configurations)
  • $CN=6$: Octahedral     $$
  • $CN=3$ with $sp^2$ hybridization

rows: Common for $d^0, d^{10}, $ and some d5 metal ions

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question: Determine the coordination number and geometry for the complex $[NiCl_4]^{2-}$.
blocks.prompt: Determine the coordination number and geometry for the complex $[NiCl_4]^{2-}$.

blocks.title: Example-2
blocks.question: What is the coordination number and geometry for the complex $[PtCl_4]^{2-}$?
blocks.prompt: What is the coordination number and geometry for the complex $[PtCl_4]^{2-}$?

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Misconception: Assuming all complexes with $CN=4$ are tetrahedral; some are square planar, especially those with $d^8$ metal ions.
  • Assuming all ligands are monodentate, leading to incorrect calculations of coordination numbers.
Recognizing the coordination number helps predict the geometry, which is crucial for understanding the properties and reactivity of coordination compounds.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Crystal Field Theory (CFT)

• Interaction between metal ions and ligands is electrostatic.

• Causes splitting of metal d-orbitals.

blocks.title: Formulas & Mathematical Relations
blocks.text:
• Crystal Field Splitting Energy ($\Delta$):
$\Delta = \Delta_o \text{ or } \Delta_t$
  • $\Delta_o$ for octahedral, $\Delta_t$ for tetrahedral complexes.
  • Influences colour and magnetic properties.
  • Crystal Field Stabilization Energy (CFSE) for Octahedral complexes
$\text{CFSE} = (n_{t_2g} \times -(0.4 \Delta)) + (n_{e_g} \times +(0.6 \Delta))$
  • $n_{t_2g}$: Electrons in t₂g orbitals.
  • $n_{e_g}$: Electrons in eg orbitals.
  • High-spin vs Low-spin:
  • High-spin when $\Delta_0 < P$ (more unpaired electrons).
  • Low-spin when $\Delta_0 > P$.

blocks.title: DATA
blocks.text:
Constants and Definitions:

Spectrochemical Series  $(I^- < Cl^- < Br^- < F^- < OH^- < H₂O < NH₃ < en < CN^- < CO)$

  • NEET Tip: For octahedral complexes, remember $\Delta_t = \frac{4}{9} \Delta_0$.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Confusing high-spin with low-spin:
  • High-spin has more unpaired electrons.
  • Misinterpreting ligand strength impact:
  • Strong field ligands cause larger $\Delta$, leading to low-spin configurations.
This format ensures clarity and alignment with the specified guidelines, making it easier for readers to comprehend the content.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Isomerism in coordination compounds arises when compounds have the same formula but different arrangements of atoms or bonds. It is classified into:

Structural Isomerism

  • Coordination Isomerism: Exchange of ligands between cationic and anionic entities.
  • Ionisation Isomerism: Different ions are produced in solution upon dissociation.
  • Hydrate Isomerism: Difference in the number of water molecules bonded to the metal ion or present as solvent molecules in the crystalline lattice.
  • Linkage Isomerism: Different donor atoms from the same ligand bind to the metal.
Stereoisomerism

  • Geometrical Isomerism: Different spatial arrangement of ligands (cis trans)
  • Optical Isomerism: Non-superimposable mirror images (enantiomers)

blocks.title: Formulas & Mathematical Relations
blocks.text:
No specific mathematical equations are involved in isomerism, but understanding the spatial orientation and connectivity is crucial.

Use VSEPR theory to predict geometry and possible isomers.

blocks.title: DATA
blocks.text: Geometrical isomers in octahedral complexes

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Misidentifying Isomer Types: Students often confuse structural with stereoisomers. Remember: structural involves connectivity, stereoisomers involve spatial arrangement.

  • Ignoring Ligand Orientation: Not all ligands can produce geometrical isomerism; focus on bidentate ligands and square planar complexes.

blocks.title: Additional Guidelines
blocks.text:
• Visualize Complexes: Use model kits or draw out complexes to see possible isomers, especially for geometrical and optical isomers.

  • Practice with NEET Questions: Familiarize with typical NEET questions like identifying possible isomers for given formulas.
Tip: Always start by identifying the coordination number and geometry to predict possible isomers effectively.
